MIC-001.q: The law of demand says that, other things equal:
MIC-001.e: The inverse price–quantity relation is a movement along the demand curve.
o: A higher price lowers quantity demanded
A higher price raises quantity demanded
MIC-001.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (Mankiw – Principles of Economics; Marshall 1890).
Analysis: The law of demand: other things equal, a higher price → lower quantity demanded – a movement along the curve. Causes: substitution effect (relatively dearer), income effect (lower real purchasing power – MIC-038) and diminishing marginal utility (MIC-031).
Distractors: B contradicts the law (only rare Giffen goods); C fails for inferior goods (MIC-016); D is wrong.

MIC-002.q: Higher consumer income makes the demand curve for a normal good:
MIC-002.e: Non-price factors shift the whole curve.
MIC-002.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (shifts versus movements along demand).
Analysis: Income is a non-price determinant → a change shifts the whole curve. For normal goods, higher income → more demand at every price → the curve shifts right. For inferior goods it shifts left (MIC-016).
Distractors: B applies to inferior goods; C – movements along come only from the good's own price; D is wrong.

MIC-003.q: Demand Qd = 100 − 2P, supply Qs = 20 + 2P. What is the equilibrium price?
MIC-003.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (market equilibrium).
Working: Qd = Qs → 100 − 2P = 20 + 2P → 80 = 4P → P = 20.
Check: Qd = 100 − 40 = 60; Qs = 20 + 40 = 60 ✓.
Analysis: At P = 20 there's no surplus or shortage; above it supply exceeds demand, below it demand exceeds supply, pushing price back.

MIC-004.q: Demand Qd = 100 − 2P, supply Qs = 20 + 2P. What is the equilibrium quantity?
MIC-004.x:
Basis: Microeconomics.
Working: Substitute P = 20 (MIC-003) into demand: Q = 100 − 2 × 20 = 60; supply check: 20 + 2 × 20 = 60 ✓.
Analysis: Equilibrium quantity is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied at the equilibrium price; substitute into both functions to check.

MIC-005.q: With Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 20 + 2P, a price ceiling of P = 15 is imposed. What is the shortage?
MIC-005.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (price ceilings).
Working: At P = 15: Qd = 100 − 30 = 70; Qs = 20 + 30 = 50; shortage = 70 − 50 = 20 units.
Analysis: A ceiling below equilibrium (20) binds → excess demand, queues, black markets, rationing by connections; actual trade equals supply of 50 (below 60) → deadweight loss.

MIC-006.q: A price floor set above equilibrium creates a surplus.
MIC-006.e: True. Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at the floor.
MIC-006.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (price floors).
Analysis: True. A floor above equilibrium → quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded → a surplus. E.g., a minimum wage above equilibrium may cause low-skill unemployment; farm price floors require the state to buy the surplus.
Note: A floor below equilibrium doesn't bind.

MIC-007.q: Petrol prices rise sharply. Demand for large-engine cars will:
MIC-007.e: A higher complement price reduces demand for the good.
o: Fall (shift left) because petrol is a complement
MIC-007.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (complements – negative cross elasticity).
Analysis: Fuel and big-engine cars are complements (used together). Higher fuel prices → higher running costs → lower demand for big-engine cars at every car price → the demand curve shifts left.
Distractors: B and C have the wrong direction; D – a movement along occurs only when the car's price changes.

MIC-008.q: Coffee prices rise sharply. Demand for tea (a substitute) will:
MIC-008.e: Consumers switch to the relatively cheaper substitute.
MIC-008.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (substitutes – positive cross elasticity).
Analysis: Coffee and tea are substitutes. Pricier coffee → tea is relatively cheaper → consumers switch → more tea demanded at every tea price → tea demand shifts right (MIC-027).
Distractors: B and C have the wrong direction; D – coffee prices don't directly cut tea supply.

MIC-009.q: Select ALL factors that SHIFT the supply curve:
MIC-009.e: The good's own price moves along the supply curve.
MIC-009.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (determinants of supply).
Analysis: Supply shifts with: (A) input prices – higher → supply falls (left); (B) technology – lower costs → right; (C) more sellers → right; (D) per-unit taxes → left (up by the tax – MIC-010), subsidies → right.
Distractors: (E) The good's own price moves along the supply curve.

MIC-010.q: Qd = 100 − 2P, Qs = 20 + 2P. A per-unit tax of 4 is levied on sellers. What price do buyers pay?
MIC-010.e: New supply: Qs = 20 + 2(P − 4) = 12 + 2P; 100 − 2P = 12 + 2P → P = 22; sellers receive 18; Q = 56.
MIC-010.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (per-unit taxes).
Working: Tax on sellers: they receive P − 4 → new supply Qs = 20 + 2(P − 4) = 12 + 2P. Equilibrium: 100 − 2P = 12 + 2P → 4P = 88 → P = 22 (buyers' price); sellers receive 22 − 4 = 18; Q = 100 − 44 = 56.
Check: 12 + 2 × 22 = 56 ✓.
Analysis: Buyers pay 2 more (from 20), sellers get 2 less – split evenly because supply and demand slopes are equal (MIC-014).

MIC-011.q: Qd = 100 − 2P, Qs = 20 + 2P. A per-unit tax of 4 is levied on sellers. What is total tax revenue?
MIC-011.e: 4 × 56 = 224. Buyers bear 2 (22 − 20) and sellers 2 (20 − 18) per unit.
MIC-011.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (tax revenue and incidence).
Working: Revenue = tax per unit × post-tax quantity = 4 × 56 = 224.
Analysis: Burden per unit: buyers 22 − 20 = 2, sellers 20 − 18 = 2. Total burden = 2 × 56 + 2 × 56 = 224 = revenue; plus a deadweight loss of 8 (MIC-013) – surplus lost to everyone.
Check: 112 + 112 = 224 ✓.

MIC-012.q: With Qd = 100 − 2P (maximum willingness to pay 50), equilibrium P = 20, Q = 60. What is consumer surplus?
MIC-012.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (consumer surplus).
Working: Choke price (Qd = 0) = 50; CS = ½ × Q × (choke − P) = ½ × 60 × (50 − 20) = ½ × 60 × 30 = 900.
Analysis: Consumer surplus is the triangle below demand and above price – the total gap between willingness to pay and the price paid (MIC-039).

MIC-013.q: Qd = 100 − 2P, Qs = 20 + 2P. A per-unit tax of 4 cuts quantity from 60 to 56. What is the deadweight loss?
MIC-013.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (deadweight loss – Harberger triangle).
Working: DWL = ½ × tax × ΔQ = ½ × 4 × (60 − 56) = ½ × 4 × 4 = 8.
Analysis: Trades where buyers value units above sellers' cost (units 57–60) no longer happen because of the tax → a loss no one receives. DWL grows with the square of the tax and is larger when supply and demand are elastic.

MIC-014.q: The economic incidence of a tax doesn't depend on whether the law makes buyers or sellers pay.
MIC-014.e: True. Incidence depends on the relative elasticities of supply and demand.
MIC-014.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (tax incidence).
Analysis: True. Whether the law makes sellers or buyers pay, the equilibrium (buyers' price, sellers' price, quantity) is the same; the real split depends only on relative elasticities (MIC-015). Statutory incidence ≠ economic incidence.
Note (application): for VAT and excise duties, firms with pricing power and inelastic demand pass more of the tax to consumers.

MIC-015.q: Which side bears most of a tax burden?
MIC-015.e: E.g., tobacco tax falls mainly on smokers because demand is inelastic.
o: The less elastic side (supply or demand)
MIC-015.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (tax incidence).
Analysis: The less elastic side bears most of the tax because it can't easily change behaviour (few substitutes or alternatives). Approximation: buyers' share = Es / (Es + |Ed|). E.g., tobacco taxes fall mainly on smokers because demand is inelastic (addiction).
Distractors: B is the reverse; C and D aren't fixed.

MIC-016.q: An inferior good is one whose:
MIC-016.e: E.g., cheap instant noodles, public transport in some markets.
o: Price is the lowest in the market
MIC-016.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (income elasticity of demand < 0).
Analysis: Inferior goods: higher income → lower demand (negative income elasticity) as consumers trade up. E.g., cheap instant noodles, low-grade rice, public transport in some markets. The concept is behavioural, not about technical quality or price level.
Distractors: B describes normal goods; C and D misdefine.
Note (investing): sellers of inferior goods can be defensive in downturns but grow slowly as incomes rise.

MIC-017.q: A 10% price rise cuts quantity demanded by 25%. What is the magnitude of price elasticity of demand?
MIC-017.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (price elasticity of demand).
Working: |Ed| = |%ΔQ / %ΔP| = |−25% / 10%| = 2.5.
Analysis: |Ed| > 1 → elastic demand: raising price cuts revenue (quantity −25% outweighs price +10%: revenue ≈ 1.10 × 0.75 − 1 = −17.5%).

MIC-018.q: When demand is elastic (|E| > 1), a price cut will:
MIC-018.e: Quantity rises proportionally more than price falls.
MIC-018.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (elasticity–revenue relationship).
Analysis: Elastic demand (|E| > 1): a price cut → quantity rises proportionally more → total revenue rises. Conversely, with inelastic demand (|E| < 1), price increases raise revenue (MIC-023).
Distractors: B and C have the wrong direction; D – quantity rises.
Note: Higher revenue doesn't guarantee higher profit – marginal cost matters too.

MIC-019.q: Price rises from 10 to 12 and quantity falls from 100 to 80. What is the midpoint elasticity magnitude (2 decimals)?
MIC-019.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (midpoint/arc elasticity).
Working: %ΔQ = (80 − 100) / [(100 + 80)/2] = −20 / 90 ≈ −22.22%; %ΔP = (12 − 10) / [(10 + 12)/2] = 2 / 11 ≈ 18.18%; |E| ≈ 22.22 / 18.18 ≈ 1.22.
Analysis: The midpoint method gives the same answer whether price rises or falls (fixing the base-point asymmetry: 20% / 20% = 1.0 going up, 25% / 16.7% = 1.5 going down).

MIC-020.q: Necessities with few substitutes usually have price-inelastic demand.
MIC-020.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (determinants of elasticity).
Analysis: True. Necessities with few substitutes (household electricity, medicines, short-run fuel) have inelastic demand: people keep buying when prices rise.
Note (investing): firms selling essential, low-substitution products have pricing power – a source of moat; utilities, however, are often price-regulated.

MIC-021.q: Income rises 5% and demand for foreign travel rises 8%. What is income elasticity of demand?
MIC-021.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (income elasticity).
Working: Ei = %ΔQ / %ΔIncome = 8% / 5% = 1.6.
Analysis: Ei > 1 → luxury (demand grows faster than income); 0 < Ei < 1 → necessity; Ei < 0 → inferior.
Note (investing): high-Ei sectors (travel, airlines, luxury) benefit strongly from income growth but are recession-sensitive – cyclical.

MIC-022.q: A negative cross-price elasticity between two goods shows they are:
MIC-022.e: A rise in one's price lowers demand for the other.
MIC-022.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (cross elasticity).
Analysis: Exy = %ΔQx / %ΔPy. Exy < 0 → a higher Y price lowers X demand → complements (fuel–cars, printers–ink). Exy > 0 → substitutes (MIC-027); Exy ≈ 0 → independent.
Distractors: B, C and D have the wrong sign or concept (inferior goods relate to income elasticity).

MIC-023.q: Price elasticity magnitude is 0.4. The firm raises price 10%. By how much does revenue change (exact, %)?
MIC-023.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (elasticity and revenue).
Working: Quantity falls 0.4 × 10% = 4%; new/old revenue = 1.10 × 0.96 = 1.056 → up 5.6% (approximation: 10% − 4% = 6%).
Analysis: Inelastic demand (|E| = 0.4 < 1) → a price rise lifts revenue. This underlies pricing power, though elasticity usually rises over time as customers find substitutes (MIC-025).

MIC-024.q: Along a linear demand curve, price elasticity is constant.
MIC-024.e: False. It's elastic at high prices and inelastic at low prices.
MIC-024.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (elasticity along a linear demand curve).
Analysis: False. A linear demand curve has a constant slope (ΔP/ΔQ) but elasticity E = (ΔQ/ΔP) × (P/Q) varies with P/Q: at high prices/low quantities |E| > 1 (elastic); at the midpoint |E| = 1 (MIC-028); at low prices |E| < 1. Don't confuse slope with elasticity.

MIC-025.q: Select ALL factors that make demand more elastic:
o: A large share of the budget
MIC-025.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (determinants of price elasticity).
Analysis: Demand is more elastic with: (A) many close substitutes; (B) a large budget share (buyers shop carefully); (C) longer adjustment time (switching to efficient cars, moving home); (D) a narrowly defined market (one brand has more substitutes than a whole category).
Distractors: (E) Necessities are usually inelastic (MIC-020).

MIC-026.q: Perfectly inelastic supply is shown by:
MIC-026.e: E.g., city-centre land in the short run.
MIC-026.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (supply elasticity).
Analysis: Perfectly inelastic supply (Es = 0): fixed quantity regardless of price → a vertical supply curve. E.g., central city land, tickets to one match, a late master's paintings. When demand rises, only price rises – why central land prices surge as cities grow.
Distractors: B is perfectly elastic; C is normal; D isn't a supply curve.

MIC-027.q: Coffee prices rise 10% and tea demand rises 3%. What is the cross-price elasticity?
MIC-027.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (cross elasticity).
Working: Exy = %ΔQ_tea / %ΔP_coffee = 3% / 10% = 0.3.
Analysis: Exy > 0 → substitutes; 0.3 is small → weak substitutes (many don't see tea as a full replacement). Used in competition analysis and defining relevant markets (competition law).

MIC-028.q: On a linear demand curve, total revenue is maximised where:
o: Elasticity is unitary (|E| = 1), at the midpoint
MIC-028.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (marginal revenue and elasticity: MR = P(1 − 1/|E|)).
Analysis: Total revenue peaks where MR = 0 ⇔ |E| = 1 – at the midpoint of a linear demand curve. Above it (|E| > 1), price cuts raise revenue; below it (|E| < 1), price rises raise revenue (MIC-029).
Distractors: B – at the choke price Q = 0, revenue is zero; C – at maximum Q, P = 0 and revenue is zero; D – zero elasticity occurs at zero price.

MIC-029.q: Demand is Qd = 100 − 2P. What price maximises total revenue?
MIC-029.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (revenue maximisation).
Working: TR = P × Q = P(100 − 2P) = 100P − 2P²; dTR/dP = 100 − 4P = 0 → P = 25; Q = 100 − 50 = 50; TR = 1,250.
Check: At P = 25: |E| = 2 × 25 / 50 = 1 ✓ (the midpoint: choke price 50, maximum quantity 100).
Analysis: Revenue maximisation differs from profit maximisation (MR = MC) unless marginal cost is zero.

MIC-030.q: Short-run supply is usually less elastic than long-run supply.
MIC-030.e: True. In the long run firms expand plants and new firms enter.
MIC-030.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (supply elasticity over time).
Analysis: True. Short run, plant capacity is fixed → supply rises only via overtime and inventories → inelastic. Long run, firms expand and newcomers enter → more elastic supply.
Note (cyclical investing): this drives commodity cycles (steel, fertiliser, rubber): prices spike when short-run supply is rigid → capacity expansion → oversupply and falling prices a few years later.

MIC-031.q: The law of diminishing marginal utility says:
MIC-031.e: It underpins the downward-sloping demand curve.
o: Each extra unit consumed adds less utility than the previous one
MIC-031.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (Gossen; marginal utility theory).
Analysis: Diminishing marginal utility: each extra unit adds less satisfaction than the previous (the first glass of water when thirsty is worth more than the fifth). Total utility still rises while MU > 0. It underpins downward-sloping demand: people buy more only at lower prices matching lower MU.
Distractors: B – total utility rises while MU > 0; C is the reverse; D isn't the law.

MIC-032.q: A consumer maximises utility over two goods: MUx = 30, Px = 10, Py = 5. At the optimum, what must MUy be?
MIC-032.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (equimarginal principle: MUx/Px = MUy/Py).
Working: 30 / 10 = MUy / 5 → MUy = 3 × 5 = 15.
Analysis: At the optimum, the last unit of money spent on each good yields equal marginal utility (3 utils per unit). If MUy/Py > MUx/Px → shift spending to Y to raise total utility (MIC-042).

MIC-033.q: With well-behaved preferences, indifference curves are convex to the origin and don't cross.
MIC-033.e: True. Convexity reflects diminishing MRS; non-crossing follows from transitivity.
MIC-033.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (preference theory – indifference curves).
Analysis: True. Convex to the origin because the marginal rate of substitution diminishes (the more X you have, the less Y you'll give up for more X). They don't cross because of transitivity and 'more is better' – crossing would make one bundle both equal to and better than another, a contradiction.

MIC-034.q: The marginal rate of substitution (MRS) equals:
MIC-034.e: At the optimum, MRS = Px/Py (the budget line slope).
o: The (absolute) slope of the indifference curve
The slope of the budget line
MIC-034.x:
Basis: Microeconomics.
Analysis: MRS = the amount of Y given up for one more X keeping utility constant = |slope of the indifference curve| = MUx/MUy. At the optimum the indifference curve is tangent to the budget line: MRS = Px/Py (subjective trade-off = market trade-off).
Distractors: B – the budget line's slope is Px/Py (MIC-035); C and D aren't the MRS.

MIC-035.q: The slope of the budget line (x on the horizontal axis) is:
MIC-035.e: It reflects the market trade-off between the two goods.
MIC-035.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (budget line: Px·X + Py·Y = I).
Analysis: Rewriting Y = I/Py − (Px/Py)·X → slope = −Px/Py: buying one more X costs Px/Py units of Y – the market trade-off. Income changes shift the line in parallel; price changes rotate it.
Distractors: B is the inverse; C is the horizontal intercept (MIC-036); D is wrong.

MIC-036.q: Income 1,000, Px = 20, Py = 50. Buying only X, what is the maximum quantity?
MIC-036.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (budget line).
Working: Only X: maximum X = I / Px = 1,000 / 20 = 50 units (horizontal intercept). Only Y: 1,000 / 50 = 20 units.
Check: Slope = −20 / 50 = −Px/Py = −20/50 = −0.4 ✓.

MIC-037.q: Match each concept with its description:
MIC-037.e: Giffen goods are rare: inferior goods with a large budget share.
p: Consumers switch to the relatively cheaper good
Real purchasing power changes when price changes
Quantity demanded rises with price due to a very strong income effect
MIC-037.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (Slutsky–Hicks decomposition; Giffen).
Analysis: Substitution effect – when a good gets cheaper, consumers switch to it as it's relatively cheaper (always opposite to price). Income effect – lower prices raise real purchasing power. Giffen good – quantity rises with price because an inferior good with a large budget share has an opposing income effect stronger than the substitution effect (very rare). Normal good – demand rises with income.

MIC-038.q: For a normal good, when price falls, both substitution and income effects raise quantity demanded.
MIC-038.e: True. For inferior goods, the income effect works in the opposite direction.
MIC-038.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (Slutsky decomposition).
Analysis: True. For a normal good, a price fall: substitution effect → buy more (relatively cheaper); income effect → real purchasing power up, buy more of a normal good → both raise quantity. For inferior goods the income effect opposes (higher real income → buy less), usually smaller than the substitution effect; if larger → a Giffen good (MIC-037).

MIC-039.e: It's the area under demand and above price.
o: The difference between buyers' willingness to pay and the price actually paid
MIC-039.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (Marshall – consumer surplus).
Analysis: Consumer surplus = willingness to pay minus price paid, summed over all units = the area below demand and above price (MIC-012). Producer surplus = the area above supply and below price.
Distractors: B – sellers' profit relates to producer surplus; C and D are wrong.

MIC-040.q: Select ALL factors that shift consumer demand:
MIC-040.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (determinants of demand).
Analysis: Demand shifts with: (A) income; (B) prices of related goods – substitutes and complements (MIC-007, MIC-008); (C) tastes and trends; (D) expectations of future prices and income (expected price rises → buying earlier, raising current demand); also the number of buyers.
Distractors: (E) Production technology affects supply (MIC-009).

MIC-041.q: Linear demand; price falls from 10 to 8 and quantity rises from 50 to 60. By how much does consumer surplus rise?
MIC-041.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (change in consumer surplus).
Working: ΔCS = rectangle (existing buyers pay less) + triangle (new buyers) = (10 − 8) × 50 + ½ × (10 − 8) × (60 − 50) = 100 + 10 = 110.
Analysis: The 100 rectangle is a transfer from sellers to buyers; the 10 triangle is new surplus from additional trades.

MIC-042.q: A rational consumer allocates the budget so marginal utility per dong spent is equal across goods.
MIC-042.e: True. Otherwise shifting spending to the higher MU/P good raises total utility.
MIC-042.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (equimarginal principle).
Analysis: True. The optimum has MUx/Px = MUy/Py = … (equal marginal utility per unit of spending). If MUx/Px > MUy/Py → moving money from Y to X raises total utility; it stops when equal, thanks to diminishing marginal utility (MIC-032).
Note: The same principle applies to capital allocation – allocate until marginal risk-adjusted expected returns are equal.

MIC-043.q: In economics, the 'short run' is a period:
MIC-043.e: It's defined by input adjustability, not the calendar.
o: In which at least one input is fixed
MIC-043.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (short run versus long run).
Analysis: The short run is a period with at least one fixed input (usually plant size, machinery); in the long run all inputs vary (MIC-058). It's about input flexibility, not the calendar: a steel mill's 'short run' spans years, a café's a few months.
Distractors: B and C use fixed calendar periods; D describes the long run.

MIC-044.q: Total cost TC = 500 + 20Q + Q². What is marginal cost at Q = 10?
MIC-044.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (marginal cost MC = dTC/dQ).
Working: MC = d(500 + 20Q + Q²)/dQ = 20 + 2Q; at Q = 10: MC = 20 + 20 = 40.
Analysis: The fixed 500 doesn't affect MC (zero derivative) → producing one more unit depends only on extra variable cost. Discrete check: TC(11) − TC(10) = 841 − 800 = 41 ≈ 40 ✓.

MIC-045.q: TC = 500 + 20Q + Q². What is average total cost at Q = 10?
MIC-045.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (average total cost ATC = TC/Q).
Working: TC(10) = 500 + 20 × 10 + 10² = 500 + 200 + 100 = 800; ATC = 800 / 10 = 80.
Analysis: ATC = AFC (500/10 = 50) + AVC (20 + 10 = 30) = 80. At Q = 10, MC (40) < ATC (80) → ATC is falling – more output lowers average cost (MIC-047).

MIC-046.q: TC = 500 + 20Q + Q². At what output is ATC minimised (2 decimals)?
MIC-046.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (minimum ATC).
Working: ATC = 500/Q + 20 + Q; dATC/dQ = −500/Q² + 1 = 0 → Q² = 500 → Q = √500 ≈ 22.36.
Check: At Q ≈ 22.36: ATC = 22.36 + 20 + 22.36 ≈ 64.72; MC = 20 + 2 × 22.36 ≈ 64.72 → MC = ATC ✓ (MIC-047).
Analysis: This is the most efficient output level for this short-run plant.

MIC-047.q: The marginal cost curve cuts average total cost at ATC's minimum.
MIC-047.e: True. When MC < ATC, ATC falls; when MC > ATC, ATC rises.
MIC-047.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (average–marginal relationship).
Analysis: True. When MC < ATC, the extra unit costs less than average → pulling ATC down; when MC > ATC → pulling it up. So MC crosses ATC (and AVC) at their minimums (MIC-046). Like an exam score below your average pulling the average down.

MIC-048.e: E.g., adding workers to a fixed production line.
o: One variable input increases while others are fixed
MIC-048.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (law of diminishing marginal returns – short run).
Analysis: It applies when one variable input (labour) rises while others are fixed (production line, building): beyond a point each added worker contributes less as machinery and space are shared (MIC-055). That's why short-run MC slopes up.
Distractors: B and C – scaling all inputs concerns economies of scale (long run – MIC-051); D – technology shifts the production function.

MIC-049.q: Fixed cost is 500 and output 25. What is average fixed cost?
MIC-049.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (average fixed cost).
Working: AFC = FC / Q = 500 / 25 = 20.
Analysis: AFC keeps falling as output rises (fixed costs are 'spread thinner') – the source of operating leverage: high-fixed-cost firms see profit grow faster than revenue when volumes rise (and the reverse in downturns).

MIC-050.q: Match each cost type with an example at a garment factory:
MIC-050.e: Sunk costs shouldn't influence future decisions.
p: Extra cost of sewing one more shirt
Design research already spent and unrecoverable
MIC-050.x:
Basis: Microeconomics; management accounting.
Analysis: Fixed cost – unchanged with output in the relevant range (factory rent). Variable cost – varies with output (fabric, thread). Marginal cost – the extra cost of one more unit. Sunk cost – spent and unrecoverable (sample design research) – shouldn't affect future decisions.
Note (investment psychology): a share's purchase cost is sunk – don't hold or sell based on it (anchoring, disposition effect).

MIC-051.e: Diseconomies arise when LRATC rises due to coordination problems.
o: Long-run average cost falls as output rises
Long-run average cost rises with output
MIC-051.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (long-run costs – LRATC).
Analysis: Economies of scale: LRATC falls as output rises (specialisation, bulk buying, spreading fixed costs – MIC-054). Diseconomies: LRATC rises from management, coordination and bureaucracy problems. Constant returns: flat LRATC.
Distractors: B describes diseconomies; C and D are unrelated.
Note (investing): scale is a moat source – industry leaders have lower unit costs (steel, retail, big banks).

MIC-052.q: Revenue 1,000; explicit costs 700; the owner gave up a salary of 200/year; own capital could earn 50 interest. What is economic profit?
MIC-052.e: Accounting profit 300; less implicit costs 250 → economic profit 50.
MIC-052.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (accounting versus economic profit).
Working: Accounting profit = 1,000 − 700 = 300; implicit (opportunity) costs = forgone salary 200 + forgone deposit interest 50 = 250; economic profit = 300 − 250 = 50.
Analysis: Positive economic profit → the business beats the best alternative. Application: EVA = NOPAT − WACC × invested capital – firms create value only when ROIC > cost of capital (the same idea as ROE > Ke in the FA Score).

MIC-053.q: When implicit (opportunity) costs exist, accounting profit exceeds economic profit.
MIC-053.e: True. Economic profit also deducts the opportunity cost of owner resources.
MIC-053.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (opportunity cost).
Analysis: True. Accounting profit = revenue − explicit (cash) costs; economic profit = accounting profit − implicit costs (opportunity cost of the owner's capital, time and assets). With positive implicit costs, accounting profit > economic profit (MIC-052).
Note (investing): accounting profit ignores the cost of equity → ROE below Ke destroys value despite accounting profits.

MIC-054.q: Select ALL sources of economies of scale:
MIC-054.e: Coordination problems cause diseconomies of scale.
o: Spreading fixed costs (R&D, advertising) over large output
Coordination problems in very large organisations
MIC-054.x:
Basis: Microeconomics; Porter (1980) – cost advantage.
Analysis: Sources of scale economies: (A) labour specialisation; (B) bulk-purchase discounts (bargaining power); (C) spreading fixed costs (R&D, advertising, systems) over large volumes; (D) cheaper borrowing (higher credit standing, size).
Distractors: (E) Coordination difficulties in very large organisations are a diseconomy (MIC-051).

MIC-055.q: Labour rises from 10 to 11 workers and output from 200 to 215. What is the marginal product of labour?
MIC-055.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (marginal product of labour).
Working: MPL = ΔQ / ΔL = (215 − 200) / (11 − 10) = 15.
Analysis: Average product falls from 20 (200/10) to ≈ 19.55 (215/11) because MPL (15) < APL (20). If MPL keeps falling as workers are added → diminishing marginal returns (MIC-048).

MIC-056.q: A cost-minimising firm: MPL = 20, wage w = 10, rental rate r = 25. At the optimum, what must MPK be?
MIC-056.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (cost minimisation: MPL/w = MPK/r).
Working: 20 / 10 = MPK / 25 → MPK = 2 × 25 = 50.
Analysis: At the optimum, the last unit of spending on each input yields the same marginal product (2 units per unit of money). If wages rise relative to the rental rate → firms substitute machines for labour (automation).

MIC-057.e: A large MES relative to the market usually means a concentrated industry.
o: The smallest output at which long-run average cost reaches its minimum
MIC-057.x:
Basis: Microeconomics; industrial organisation (Scherer).
Analysis: MES – the smallest output at which LRATC reaches its minimum. If MES is large relative to the market (steel, refining, cement) → only a few firms can be efficient → a concentrated industry (oligopoly); a small MES (restaurants) → many firms.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the definition.
Note (industry analysis): a high MES is an entry barrier supporting incumbents' sustained profits.

MIC-058.q: In the long run, all costs are variable.
MIC-058.e: True. The firm can adjust all inputs.
MIC-058.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (long run).
Analysis: True. The long run is long enough to adjust every input (expanding or shrinking plants, entering or exiting) → no fixed costs, all costs variable (MIC-043). The long-run decision: whether to stay in the industry (P ≥ minimum LRATC).

MIC-059.q: A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker, so:
MIC-059.e: The firm's demand curve is horizontal at the market price.
o: It can set a high price
It earns positive long-run economic profit
MIC-059.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (perfect competition).
Analysis: A perfectly competitive firm is tiny relative to the market with a homogeneous product → a price taker; its demand curve is horizontal at P → each extra unit earns exactly P: P = MR = AR. Profit is maximised at P = MC (MIC-060).
Distractors: B – no pricing power; C – market demand slopes down, firm demand is flat; D – long-run economic profit is zero (MIC-063).

MIC-060.q: A perfectly competitive firm: market price 50, MC = 10 + 2Q. What output maximises profit?
MIC-060.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (profit maximisation MR = MC).
Working: Under perfect competition MR = P: 50 = 10 + 2Q → 2Q = 40 → Q = 20.
Analysis: Below 20, P > MC so more output adds profit; above 20, MC > P so extra units lose money. Also check P ≥ minimum AVC to avoid shutdown (MIC-062).

MIC-061.q: A perfectly competitive firm: TC = 100 + 10Q + Q², market price P = 50. What is maximum profit?
MIC-061.x:
Basis: Microeconomics.
Working: MC = 10 + 2Q = 50 → Q = 20; TR = 50 × 20 = 1,000; TC = 100 + 10 × 20 + 20² = 100 + 200 + 400 = 700; profit = 1,000 − 700 = 300.
Check: ATC = 700 / 20 = 35 < P = 50 → profit per unit 15 × 20 = 300 ✓.
Analysis: Positive economic profit attracts entry → in the long run price falls to minimum ATC and profit to zero (MIC-063).

MIC-062.q: In the short run, a firm should shut down temporarily when:
MIC-062.e: If AVC ≤ P < ATC, it should keep producing to cover part of fixed costs.
o: Price is below minimum average variable cost (P < min AVC)
Price is below average total cost
MIC-062.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (short-run shutdown condition).
Analysis: In the short run, fixed costs are paid regardless (sunk for short-run decisions). Shut down temporarily when P < minimum AVC – revenue doesn't cover variable costs. If AVC ≤ P < ATC: keep producing, as the margin over AVC covers part of fixed costs, losing less than shutting.
Distractors: B – production may continue with P < ATC; C and D aren't the criterion.
Note (cyclicals): steel and cement firms in downturns often run at low utilisation, accepting accounting losses rather than idling kilns.

MIC-063.q: In long-run perfect competition, a firm's economic profit is zero.
MIC-063.e: True. Free entry and exit eliminate economic profit.
MIC-063.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (long-run competitive equilibrium).
Analysis: True. Positive economic profit → entry → more supply, lower price; losses → exit → higher price. Long-run equilibrium at P = MC = minimum ATC → zero economic profit (accounting profit still positive, covering opportunity costs – MIC-053).
Note (investing): industries without entry barriers and with homogeneous products struggle to sustain high ROE – a durable moat is needed for ROE > Ke over time.

MIC-064.q: A monopolist faces P = 100 − Q with constant MC = 20. What is the profit-maximising price?
MIC-064.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (monopoly – MR = MC).
Working: TR = (100 − Q)Q → MR = 100 − 2Q; MR = MC → 100 − 2Q = 20 → Q = 40; P = 100 − 40 = 60.
Analysis: The monopolist sets output where MR = MC, then charges the highest price buyers accept on the demand curve. Versus competition (P = MC = 20, Q = 80): higher price, lower output.
Check: |E| at P = 60, Q = 40 = 60/40 = 1.5 > 1 ✓ (MIC-070).

MIC-065.q: A monopolist faces P = 100 − Q with constant MC = 20 and no fixed cost. What is maximum monopoly profit?
MIC-065.x:
Basis: Microeconomics.
Working: Profit = (P − MC) × Q = (60 − 20) × 40 = 1,600 (no fixed cost).
Analysis: The 1,600 monopoly profit is consumer surplus transferred to the monopolist (the rectangle); society also loses an 800 deadweight loss (MIC-066). It lasts only with entry barriers (MIC-069).

MIC-066.q: A monopolist faces P = 100 − Q with constant MC = 20. Compared with competition (P = MC), what is the deadweight loss from monopoly?
MIC-066.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (monopoly deadweight loss).
Working: Competition: P = MC = 20 → Q = 80. Monopoly: Q = 40, P = 60. DWL = ½ × (80 − 40) × (60 − 20) = ½ × 40 × 40 = 800.
Analysis: 40 units valued above their cost of 20 aren't produced → an efficiency loss. That's the rationale for competition law and monopoly regulation (MIC-071).

MIC-067.q: What is the Lerner index L = (P − MC)/P with P = 60, MC = 20 (2 decimals)?
MIC-067.x:
Basis: Lerner (1934) – market power index.
Working: L = (P − MC) / P = (60 − 20) / 60 = 40 / 60 ≈ 0.67.
Analysis: L = 0 under perfect competition; nearer 1 means more pricing power. For a profit maximiser L = 1/|E| → |E| = 1.5 (matching MIC-064).
Note (investing): high, stable gross margins through the cycle are a practical sign of pricing power.

MIC-068.e: Hard in practice; big data brings it closer (personalised pricing).
o: Each customer pays their maximum willingness to pay; the firm captures all consumer surplus
MIC-068.x:
Basis: Pigou (1920) – first-, second- and third-degree price discrimination.
Analysis: First-degree (perfect) discrimination: each customer pays their maximum willingness → the firm captures all consumer surplus with output at the competitive level (no DWL). Hard in practice; big data brings it closer (personalised pricing).
Distractors: B is second-degree (by quantity); C is third-degree (by group – MIC-073); D is uniform pricing.

MIC-069.q: Select ALL entry barriers that can create monopoly:
MIC-069.e: Many small firms characterise competitive markets.
o: Many small firms in the industry
MIC-069.x:
Basis: Microeconomics; Porter (1980) – entry barriers.
Analysis: Monopoly-creating barriers: (A) large scale economies – natural monopoly (power transmission, water); (B) patents and copyrights; (C) control of key resources (mines); (D) state licences and regulation (administrative monopoly).
Distractors: (E) Many small firms characterise competitive markets.
Note (investing): entry barriers underpin durable moats – assess their durability as law and technology change.

MIC-070.q: A profit-maximising monopolist always produces on the inelastic part of demand.
MIC-070.e: False. Since MR = MC > 0, it produces on the elastic part (|E| > 1).
MIC-070.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (MR = P(1 − 1/|E|)).
Analysis: False. A profit-maximising monopolist sets MR = MC > 0. Since MR = P(1 − 1/|E|) > 0 ⇔ |E| > 1 → it always operates on the elastic part of demand. On the inelastic part (MR < 0), cutting output and raising price both raises revenue and cuts cost → always better.

MIC-071.q: A common regulation for natural monopolies (power transmission, water) is:
MIC-071.e: MC pricing may cause losses because MC < ATC.
o: Average-cost pricing or a price cap with quality requirements
Splitting into many firms competing on the same physical network
MIC-071.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (regulating natural monopolies); Price Law 2023; price-cap practice (Littlechild, UK).
Analysis: Natural monopolies (LRATC falling across market demand, MC < ATC): MC pricing causes losses (needs subsidy); common approaches: average-cost ceilings (cost-plus with an allowed return) or CPI − X price caps with quality requirements – encouraging cost cuts.
Distractors: B – splitting one physical network loses scale economies; C invites abuse of monopoly power; D is impractical.
Note (utilities investing): profits depend on state pricing mechanisms – policy risk.

MIC-072.q: A firm with market power faces |E| = 3 and MC = 40. By the markup rule, what is the optimal price?
MIC-072.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (markup pricing rule).
Working: From MR = P(1 − 1/|E|) = MC → P = MC / (1 − 1/|E|) = 40 / (1 − 1/3) = 40 / (2/3) = 60.
Check: Lerner = (60 − 40)/60 = 1/3 = 1/|E| ✓.
Analysis: The less elastic the demand (|E| near 1), the higher the markup; as |E| → ∞ (perfect competition), P → MC.

MIC-073.q: An airline charges business travellers high fares and early-booking leisure travellers low fares. This is:
MIC-073.e: Conditions: segment customers and prevent resale.
o: Third-degree price discrimination – higher prices for the less elastic group
MIC-073.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (third-degree price discrimination).
Analysis: Airlines split customers by elasticity: business travellers (inelastic – employer pays, urgent) pay high fares; early-booking leisure travellers (elastic) pay low → third-degree discrimination, charging more to the inelastic group (MIC-072). Conditions: market power, the ability to segment (advance purchase, change rules) and to prevent resale (named tickets).
Distractors: B – prices aren't individual; C and D are wrong.

MIC-074.q: In the long run, perfectly competitive firms produce at minimum average cost.
MIC-074.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (productive and allocative efficiency).
Analysis: True. Long-run competitive equilibrium: P = minimum ATC (zero economic profit – MIC-063) → productive efficiency (lowest-cost production); also P = MC → allocative efficiency (output where marginal social value = marginal cost). Monopolistic competition doesn't achieve this (MIC-088).

MIC-075.e: Firms have some pricing power through differentiation.
o: Many firms, differentiated products, free entry; zero long-run economic profit with excess capacity
MIC-075.x:
Basis: Chamberlin (1933) – monopolistic competition.
Analysis: Monopolistic competition: many firms with differentiated products (brand, location, quality) → each has some pricing power (downward-sloping demand); free entry → zero long-run economic profit, output below minimum ATC → excess capacity (MIC-088).
Distractors: B is monopoly; C is perfect competition; D fits monopoly/oligopoly.

MIC-076.q: Match each market structure with a typical example:
MIC-076.e: Classification depends on number of firms, product differentiation and entry barriers.
p: A wholesale market for homogeneous produce
MIC-076.x:
Basis: Microeconomics; industrial organisation.
Analysis: Perfect competition – many sellers, homogeneous product (wholesale produce markets). Monopolistic competition – many sellers, differentiated products, easy entry (cafés, restaurants). Oligopoly – few large interdependent firms, high barriers (mobile telecoms, construction steel). Monopoly – one firm (national power transmission – EVNNPT).
Note: Industry structure analysis (Porter's five forces) is step 2 of the stock screening process.

MIC-077.q: A Nash equilibrium is a situation where:
MIC-077.e: It's not necessarily collectively optimal (e.g., the prisoner's dilemma).
o: Each player's strategy is a best response to the others'; no one wants to deviate unilaterally
MIC-077.x:
Basis: Nash (1950) – game theory.
Analysis: Nash equilibrium: each player chooses their best strategy given others' strategies → no one wants to deviate unilaterally. It needn't be collectively optimal – the prisoner's dilemma (MIC-078, MIC-085): both 'defect' though mutual cooperation is better.
Distractors: B describes Pareto/joint optimum; C and D aren't the definition.

MIC-078.q: Two firms agree to keep prices high. In a one-shot prisoner's dilemma, the likely outcome is:
MIC-078.e: In repeated games, cooperation can be sustained by punishment strategies.
o: Both cut prices (cheat) because it's a dominant strategy
MIC-078.x:
Basis: Game theory (prisoner's dilemma); Axelrod (1984) – repeated games.
Analysis: One-shot game: whether the rival holds or cuts, each firm does better by cutting (gaining share or avoiding losing it) → cutting is dominant → both cut, breaking the deal. In infinitely repeated games, cooperation can be sustained by punishment strategies (tit-for-tat, trigger).
Distractors: B isn't a one-shot equilibrium; C and D are wrong.

MIC-079.q: Cartels tend to be unstable because each member has an incentive to cheat and exceed its quota.
MIC-079.e: True. Price-fixing agreements are also usually banned by competition law.
MIC-079.x:
Basis: Microeconomics; Competition Law 2018 (prohibited anti-competitive agreements).
Analysis: True. Cartels resemble the prisoner's dilemma: with everyone keeping quotas, prices are high, and each member is tempted to sell more secretly at that price → cartels tend to break down (e.g., OPEC members often exceed quotas). Price-fixing and market-sharing agreements are also banned (Competition Law 2018 Arts. 11–12).

MIC-080.q: Cournot duopoly with identical firms: market demand P = 120 − Q, MC = 0. What is the equilibrium price?
MIC-080.e: Reaction: q₁ = (120 − q₂)/2; symmetric q = 40 each; Q = 80; P = 40.
MIC-080.x:
Basis: Cournot (1838) – quantity competition.
Working: Firm 1 profit: (120 − q₁ − q₂)q₁; FOC: 120 − 2q₁ − q₂ = 0 → q₁ = (120 − q₂)/2. Symmetric q₁ = q₂ = q: q = (120 − q)/2 → 3q = 120 → q = 40; Q = 80; P = 120 − 80 = 40.
Analysis: Compare: monopoly Q = 60, P = 60; perfect competition Q = 120, P = 0 (MC = 0). Cournot is in between – more firms → closer to competition.

MIC-081.q: Bertrand model: two firms sell identical products, compete on price, constant MC = 30, no capacity limits. What is the equilibrium price?
MIC-081.e: Undercutting continues until P = MC = 30 (the 'Bertrand paradox').
MIC-081.x:
Basis: Bertrand (1883) – price competition.
Working: With a homogeneous product and no capacity limits, the lower-priced firm takes the whole market → each undercuts the other until P = MC = 30 (no further cut without losses).
Analysis: The 'Bertrand paradox' – just two firms yield the competitive outcome. In practice profits survive via differentiation, capacity limits and repeated play.

MIC-082.q: Select ALL factors that facilitate tacit collusion:
MIC-082.e: Frequent entry makes collusion hard to sustain.
MIC-082.x:
Basis: Industrial organisation (Tirole; Ivaldi et al. 2003 – factors facilitating tacit collusion).
Analysis: Tacit collusion is easier with: (A) few firms – easy coordination and monitoring; (B) homogeneous products – easy price alignment; (C) repeated interaction – deviators can be punished; (D) transparent prices – fast detection of cuts.
Distractors: (E) Continuous entry undermines collusion (newcomers don't join and push prices down).

MIC-083.q: The kinked demand curve model explains:
MIC-083.e: Limitation: it doesn't explain how the initial price was set.
o: Price rigidity in oligopoly: rivals match price cuts but not rises
MIC-083.x:
Basis: Sweezy (1939); Hall & Hitch (1939) – kinked demand curve.
Analysis: In oligopoly, rivals match price cuts (to keep share) but not increases (to win customers) → demand is elastic above and inelastic below the current price → a gap in MR → MC shifts within the gap don't change price → sticky prices.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.
Note: Limitation – it doesn't explain how the initial price was set.

MIC-084.q: A dominant strategy is best regardless of what the rival chooses.
MIC-084.e: True. If all players have one, that's a dominant-strategy equilibrium.
MIC-084.x:
Basis: Game theory.
Analysis: True. A dominant strategy is a player's best choice whatever the rival does. If every player has one → a dominant-strategy equilibrium (also a Nash equilibrium), e.g., (Ad, Ad) in MIC-085. Not every game has dominant strategies; then the broader Nash concept applies.

MIC-085.q: Firms A and B choose Advertise (Ad) or Not (N). Profits (A, B): Ad–Ad (5, 5); Ad–N (12, 2); N–Ad (2, 12); N–N (10, 10). The Nash equilibrium is:
MIC-085.e: Ad is each firm's dominant strategy (12 > 10 and 5 > 2) → (Ad, Ad), though both lose versus (N, N).
MIC-085.x:
Basis: Game theory (prisoner's dilemma).
Analysis: For A: if B advertises, A gets 5 by advertising vs 2 by not; if B doesn't, A gets 12 vs 10 → advertising is A's dominant strategy; likewise for B (symmetric). Nash equilibrium: (Ad, Ad) = (5, 5), although both not advertising (10, 10) is better – a collectively suboptimal outcome.
Distractors: B – (No, No) is unstable since each wants to deviate to Ad; C is unstable; D – an equilibrium exists.

MIC-086.q: Firms A and B choose Advertise (Ad) or Not (N). Profits (A, B): Ad–Ad (5, 5); Ad–N (12, 2); N–Ad (2, 12); N–N (10, 10). How much joint profit is lost at the Nash equilibrium versus both not advertising?
MIC-086.x:
Basis: Game theory.
Working: Total profit at (No, No) = 10 + 10 = 20; at Nash (Ad, Ad) = 5 + 5 = 10; lost = 20 − 10 = 10.
Analysis: Competitive advertising largely cancels out (stealing each other's customers) → an 'arms race' hurting the industry. That's why some industries welcome advertising bans/limits (tobacco) – effectively an escape from the dilemma.

MIC-087.q: In the Stackelberg model, the leader:
MIC-087.e: Committing to output first forces the rival to adapt.
o: Enjoys a first-mover advantage, producing more and earning more than under Cournot
Is always worse off than the follower
MIC-087.x:
Basis: Stackelberg (1934) – leadership model.
Analysis: The leader commits to output first, anticipating the follower's reaction function → chooses more than Cournot, forcing the follower to cut back → the leader earns more and the follower less than under Cournot (first-mover advantage). With MIC-080's demand: leader 60, follower 30, P = 30.
Distractors: B is the reverse; C is a different price-leadership model; D is wrong.

MIC-088.q: In long-run monopolistic competition, firms set P = ATC but produce below the minimum-ATC output.
MIC-088.e: True. Downward-sloping demand is tangent to ATC on its falling part → excess capacity.
MIC-088.x:
Basis: Chamberlin (1933) – excess capacity theorem.
Analysis: True. In long-run monopolistic competition, free entry pushes economic profit to zero → P = ATC; but downward-sloping demand touches ATC only where ATC is still falling → output below minimum-ATC level → excess capacity and P > MC (neither productive nor allocative efficiency – MIC-074). The price of product variety.

MIC-089.q: With a negative externality (e.g., pollution), a free market usually:
MIC-089.e: Marginal social cost exceeds marginal private cost.
o: Overproduces relative to the social optimum
MIC-089.x:
Basis: Pigou (1920) – externalities.
Analysis: Negative externality: marginal social cost (MSC) = private cost (MPC) + external cost (MEC) > MPC. Firms decide on MPC → produce until MPC = P, above the social optimum (MSC = P) → overproduction and excess pollution. Remedies: Pigouvian tax (MIC-090), emissions trading (MIC-098), standards.
Distractors: B applies to positive externalities (MIC-096); C and D are wrong.

MIC-090.q: Each tonne of cement causes a constant external pollution cost of 15. What is the optimal Pigouvian tax per tonne?
MIC-090.e: The Pigouvian tax equals marginal external cost at the optimal output.
MIC-090.x:
Basis: Pigou (1920) – Pigouvian tax.
Working: Optimal Pigouvian tax = marginal external cost at the optimal output = 15 per tonne (constant external cost).
Analysis: The tax makes firms 'internalise' the externality: MPC + 15 = MSC → market output moves to the social optimum. Revenue can cut other taxes (the 'double dividend'). Vietnam's Environmental Protection Tax (2010 law) follows this logic.

MIC-091.e: E.g., national defence, street lighting; prone to free-riding.
MIC-091.x:
Basis: Samuelson (1954) – public goods.
Analysis: Pure public goods: non-rival (one person's use doesn't reduce another's) and non-excludable (non-payers can't be kept out). E.g., defence, street lighting, lighthouses → the free-rider problem (MIC-099) → private under-provision → usually tax-financed by the state.
Distractors: B describes private goods; C – private firms can produce them under contract; D – they still cost money (funded by taxes).

MIC-092.q: The Coase theorem says that with clear property rights and low transaction costs, parties can bargain to an efficient outcome regardless of initial allocation.
MIC-092.e: True. In practice transaction costs are often high with many parties.
MIC-092.x:
Basis: Coase (1960), 'The Problem of Social Cost'.
Analysis: True. With clear property rights and low transaction costs, parties bargain (the polluter compensates, or the affected pay for abatement) → an efficient outcome regardless of who holds the initial right (which only affects distribution). In practice, transaction costs are high with many parties (city-wide air pollution) → state intervention is needed.

MIC-093.q: Match each asymmetric information concept with an example:
MIC-093.e: Adverse selection occurs before the contract; moral hazard after.
p: People in poorer health are more likely to buy health insurance
Drivers become careless after buying car damage insurance
A firm offers a 5-year warranty to prove quality
An insurer requires a medical check before contracting
MIC-093.x:
Basis: Akerlof (1970) – the market for 'lemons'; Spence (1973) – signalling; Rothschild & Stiglitz (1976) – screening.
Analysis: Adverse selection (pre-contract) – people in poor health buy more insurance, knowing their risk. Moral hazard (post-contract) – driving carelessly once insured. Signalling – the informed party (firm) proves quality (5-year warranty). Screening – the uninformed party (insurer) requires health checks.
Note (investing): dividends, buybacks and insider purchases are signals the market still needs to verify.

MIC-094.q: Select ALL measures that limit adverse selection in insurance:
o: Menus with different deductibles for self-selection
Universal mandatory insurance creating a broad pool
MIC-094.x:
Basis: Information economics (Rothschild & Stiglitz 1976).
Analysis: Curbing adverse selection: (A) health checks and risk underwriting (screening); (B) menus with different deductibles for self-selection – revealing risk (low-risk buyers pick high deductibles, low premiums); (C) universal mandatory insurance (social health insurance) creating a broad pool; (D) waiting periods for some benefits – preventing purchase after diagnosis.
Distractors: (E) Less information worsens the asymmetry.

MIC-095.q: The 'tragedy of the commons' is best illustrated by:
MIC-095.e: Rival but non-excludable resources get depleted; quotas or use rights are needed.
MIC-095.x:
Basis: Hardin (1968), 'The Tragedy of the Commons'; Ostrom (1990).
Analysis: Common-pool resources: rival (a fish caught isn't available to others) but hard to exclude (open sea) → each user over-harvests since depletion costs are shared → overexploitation. Solutions: quotas, tradable fishing rights, community management (Ostrom).
Distractors: B, C and D aren't common-pool resources.

MIC-096.q: Vaccination: marginal private benefit MPB = 50 − Q; constant marginal external benefit 10; marginal cost 20. What is the socially optimal quantity?
MIC-096.e: Market: 50 − Q = 20 → Q = 30. Social: (50 − Q) + 10 = 20 → Q = 40; a subsidy of 10 per unit can achieve it.
MIC-096.x:
Basis: Microeconomics (positive externality – Pigouvian subsidy).
Working: Market: MPB = MC → 50 − Q = 20 → Q = 30. Social: MSB = MPB + 10 = 60 − Q = 20 → Q = 40.
Analysis: The positive externality (vaccinees reduce others' infection) → market under-provision (30 < 40). A subsidy of 10 per unit (equal to the marginal external benefit) makes MPB + 10 = MC at Q = 40 – the social optimum.
Check: 60 − 40 = 20 = MC ✓.

MIC-097.q: Government intervention to fix market failures can also cause 'government failure' and worsen outcomes.
MIC-097.e: True. Due to information gaps, interest groups and administrative costs.
MIC-097.x:
Basis: Public economics; Buchanan & Tullock (1962) – public choice.
Analysis: True. Government failure: poor information (external costs unknown), lobbying and rent-seeking, short-term political motives, administrative costs, corruption → intervention can worsen outcomes versus the original market failure. Compare the costs and benefits of intervention against reality, not an ideal.

MIC-098.e: Permit prices are set by the market; total quantity is fixed with certainty.
o: Sets a total cap and allocates tradable permits; cuts happen where cheapest
Levies a flat tax on all firms
MIC-098.x:
Basis: Environmental economics (Dales 1968; Montgomery 1972); EU ETS; Environmental Protection Law 2020 and Decree 06/2022/ND-CP (Vietnam's carbon market roadmap).
Analysis: Cap-and-trade: the state sets a total emissions cap and allocates/auctions allowances that firms can trade → low-abatement-cost firms cut emissions and sell surplus allowances; high-cost firms buy → the total cut is achieved at least social cost. Versus taxes (fixed price, uncertain quantity), cap-and-trade fixes quantity with market-set prices.
Distractors: B is a tax; C is infeasible; D defeats the goal.

MIC-099.e: It leads to under-provision of public goods by the private sector.
o: Beneficiaries don't pay because they can't be excluded
MIC-099.x:
Basis: Olson (1965) – the free-rider problem; Samuelson (1954).
Analysis: Free riders benefit from non-excludable goods without paying (neighbourhood security, street lighting) → everyone waits for others to pay → private under-provision (MIC-091) → tax financing or mandatory schemes are needed.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't free-riding.
Note: In corporate governance, small shareholders free-ride on monitoring by large holders/funds – one reason governance is weak where ownership is dispersed.

MIC-100.q: A plant emits 500 tonnes of CO₂ and holds 400 tonnes of permits; the permit price is 40 per tonne. Without abatement, what does it cost to buy the extra permits?
MIC-100.e: (500 − 400) × 40 = 4,000; if abatement costs under 40/tonne, the plant should cut emissions itself.
MIC-100.x:
Basis: Environmental economics (cap-and-trade – MIC-098).
Working: Excess emissions = 500 − 400 = 100 tonnes; cost to buy = 100 × 40 = 4,000.
Analysis: Optimal choice: compare marginal abatement cost with the allowance price of 40 – abate until the next tonne costs 40, buy allowances for the rest. If abatement costs under 40 per tonne, cutting is cheaper than buying; it may even pay to cut further and sell surplus allowances.
Note (investing): carbon prices are a new cost for heavy emitters (steel, cement, coal power) – factor them into long-term earnings forecasts once Vietnam's carbon market operates.
